```{python}
#| label: setup
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path.cwd()))
from IPython.display import Markdown, display

import figures as F
import paperdata as D
from paperdata import (bn, count, fy, gbp, listing, md_table, num, ordinal, pct, points, pm, rate, wk, words)
from paperdata import V2  # facts about the method (versions, dates), not results

FINAL, SWITCH = D.FINAL, D.SWITCH
MID = D.DIST_YEARS[0]  # five rises after the switch
FLOOR = D.FLOOR_TEXT
TENTH = num(100 * 10 ** -D.RATE_DECIMALS, 1)  # the inputs' published precision, in points
TLL, BPL = D.LABELS["triple_lock"], D.LABELS["burnham_2030"]
DWP_TEXT = (D.ROOT / D.DWP["file"]).read_text()


def lower1(t):
    return t[0].lower() + t[1:]


# Headline figures: the expected saving over the model's paths, and the OBR central forecast.
g_final, n_final = D.est("gross", FINAL), D.est("net", FINAL)
g_mid, n_mid = D.est("gross", MID), D.est("net", MID)
lose_final = D.est("households_losing_pct", FINAL)
spread80 = D.spread80("gross", FINAL)
spread80n = D.spread80("net", FINAL)
central = D.path("central")
c_final = D.row(central, FINAL)
gap = D.EV["gap_by_calibration"][D.PRIMARY]
dwp_nominal = D.DWP["saving_bn"][str(FINAL)]["nominal"]
dwp_real = D.DWP["saving_bn"][str(FINAL)]["real_2025_26_prices"]
dwp_quote = re.search(r"In any given year it will go up by.*?that value", DWP_TEXT).group(0)
obr_premium, _ = D.obr_premium_text()
prem = D.premium()
dry = D.R["release"]["c2_dry_run"]
N_PATHS, N_RUNS = count(D.EV["draws"]["n"]), count(D.n_unique())
# The typical path: the one nearest the middle of the distribution of the final-year gap. Its saving is close to the
# average, so the household results use it.
TYP = D.path("monthly_p50")
t_final = D.row(TYP, FINAL)
PATH_NAMES = {"central": "OBR central forecast", "random": "example path (random)",
              "monthly_p50": "typical path (median saving)", "monthly_p90": "high-saving path (90th percentile)"}


def pov_change(p, k):
    """Percentage points: the plan's poverty rate less the triple lock's, in the final year."""
    return p["poverty_pct"]["burnham_2030"][str(FINAL)][k] - p["poverty_pct"]["triple_lock"][str(FINAL)][k]


pov_typ_abs, pov_typ_rel = pov_change(TYP, "pensioners_absolute_ahc"), pov_change(TYP, "pensioners_relative_ahc")
pov_c_max = max(abs(pov_change(central, k)) for k in central["poverty_pct"]["triple_lock"][str(FINAL)])
```

## Summary {.unnumbered}

::: {.summary-box}
On 29 September 2026 the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, said he would keep the State Pension triple lock until 2030 and then replace it with a rise of at least prices or `{python} FLOOR` that "will hold its value relative to earnings over time" [@bbc_live2026]. We compare this Burnham plan, as DWP describes it [@dwp_uprating2026], with the triple lock (current law) from `{python} fy(D.YEARS[0])` to `{python} fy(FINAL)`, using full PolicyEngine UK runs of the whole survey population.

**What it saves.** Averaged over `{python} N_PATHS` simulated paths of prices and earnings centred on the OBR's forecast, the plan lowers State Pension spending by `{python} bn(g_final["mean"], 1)` in `{python} fy(FINAL)`, or `{python} bn(n_final["mean"], 1)` once income tax and benefits respond. On the middle 80% of paths the gross saving runs from `{python} bn(spread80[0], 1)` to `{python} bn(spread80[1], 1)`. DWP's costing is £`{python} dwp_nominal`bn.

**Why the path matters.** The plan saves money only after years in which prices or the `{python} FLOOR` floor beat earnings. On the OBR's smooth central forecast that hardly happens, so the saving there is `{python} bn(c_final["gross"], 1)`. Real years vary, and the saving can never fall below zero, so the average over many paths is far above the saving on the average path.

**Who is affected.** About `{python} pct(lose_final["mean"], 0)` of UK households, nearly all of them with a pensioner, have less income than under the triple lock in `{python} fy(FINAL)`. Pension Credit and income tax make up part of the difference. On the typical path, whose saving is close to the average, pensioner poverty after housing costs is up to `{python} num(max(pov_typ_abs, pov_typ_rel), 1)` percentage points higher than under the triple lock.

These results are provisional: the model of prices and earnings passes the test we set in advance in a dry run on today's data, and the binding test runs on the 28 October 2026 Budget forecast.
:::

## Introduction {#sec-intro}

Since 2011 the triple lock has raised the State Pension each April by the highest of CPI inflation, earnings growth and `{python} FLOOR`. Because it takes the highest of three figures every year, a year in which prices or the floor run ahead of earnings raises the pension for good, and later rises build on the higher level. The OBR's long-term projections assume that the triple lock raises the pension `{python} obr_premium` percentage points a year faster than earnings [@obr_lted2026].

On 29 September 2026 the Prime Minister said he would keep the triple lock until 2030 and then change it, so that the pension rises every year by at least prices or `{python} FLOOR` and "will hold its value relative to earnings over time" [@bbc_live2026]. DWP's analysis published the same day says that from April `{python} SWITCH` the pension keeps the record value relative to earnings it reaches under the triple lock: "`{python} dwp_quote`" [@dwp_uprating2026]. We call this rule the Burnham plan.

This paper asks what the Burnham plan would save against the triple lock (current law), and who would be affected. Its answer has three parts. First, the saving depends on how prices and earnings move from year to year, not just on their average, so we estimate it over many possible paths rather than one. Second, on those paths the plan saves `{python} bn(g_final["mean"], 1)` in State Pension spending in `{python} fy(FINAL)` on average, and `{python} bn(n_final["mean"], 1)` after tax and benefits respond. Third, the cost to households falls almost entirely on pensioners, with Pension Credit and income tax making up part of it.

@sec-rules sets out the two rules and how the saving arises. @sec-budget gives the saving, with single scenarios and other published costings. @sec-paths follows both rules along the OBR's forecast and simulated paths. @sec-households turns to households. @sec-method describes the method, @sec-limits its limitations, and @sec-conclusion concludes.

## The triple lock and the Burnham plan {#sec-rules}

```{python}
rec = D.tl_record()
first, last = rec[0], rec[-1]
counts = {k: sum(r["binding"] == k for r in rec) for k in ("cpi", "earnings", "floor")}
idx = last["index"]
rise = {k: 100 * (idx[k] - 1) for k in idx}
above_earn = 100 * (idx["triple_lock"] / idx["earnings"] - 1)
susp_year = D.HISTORY["suspended_earnings_year"]
susp = next(r for r in rec if r["year"] == susp_year)
first_group = next(g for g in D.history_groups() if g["changes"])
unchanged = [g for g in D.history_groups() if not g["changes"]]
last_hist = D.HISTORY["model_years"][-1]
past_weekly = first_group["model"]["counterfactual_weekly"]["new_state_pension"][str(last_hist)]
actual_weekly = first_group["model"]["actual_weekly"]["new_state_pension"][str(last_hist)]
past_saving = first_group["model"]["saving_bn"][str(last_hist)]
spike = max(rec, key=lambda r: r["cpi"])
```

### The two rules

Under the triple lock the full basic and new State Pension rise each April by the highest of three figures: the CPI 12-month rate for the previous September [@ons_d7g7]; growth in average weekly earnings, whole-economy total pay, in May to July of the previous year [@ons_kac3]; and `{python} FLOOR`. The law requires only that the pension keeps up with earnings [@ssaa1992_s150a]; the prices leg and the floor are policy on top. ONS publishes both inputs to `{python} TENTH` point, and both rules here use them at that precision.

The Burnham plan follows the triple lock to April `{python} SWITCH - 1`. From April `{python} SWITCH` let $L_t$ be the pension's level and $A_t$ an earnings path that starts at the `{python} fy(SWITCH - 1)` level and grows with May–July earnings, $A_t = A_{t-1}(1 + e_{t-1})$. Then

$$L_t = \max\bigl(L_{t-1}\,(1 + \max(c_{t-1}, f)),\; A_t\bigr),$$

where $c$ is September CPI, $e$ is May–July earnings growth and $f$ is the `{python} FLOOR` floor. The pension never rises by less than the higher of CPI and the floor, and never falls below its earnings path. Any top-up to the earnings path is rounded up to `{python} TENTH` point.

### Where the saving comes from

When earnings lead, both rules give the same rise. The rules part only after a year in which the higher of CPI and `{python} FLOOR` beats earnings. Both pay that higher figure, but it lifts the plan above its earnings path. When earnings lead again, the triple lock rises with earnings from the higher level, while the plan rises only by the higher of CPI and the floor until earnings catch up. The triple lock carries each such year forward for good; the plan does not. So the saving depends on how often the lead passes between prices and earnings, and every such year can only add to it.

### The triple lock since 2011

@fig-history replays the triple lock on the published inputs for each April from `{python} first["year"]` to `{python} last["year"]`. CPI set the rise `{python} words(counts["cpi"])` times, earnings `{python} words(counts["earnings"])` times and the floor `{python} words(counts["floor"])` times. Over those rises the pension rose by `{python} pct(rise["triple_lock"], 0)` in all, against `{python} pct(rise["earnings"], 0)` for earnings alone and `{python} pct(rise["cpi"], 0)` for prices alone, which leaves it `{python} pct(above_earn, 1)` above where an earnings link alone would have taken it. In April `{python} susp_year` the law suspended the earnings leg, whose input was `{python} rate(susp["earnings"])`, so that year's rise was CPI, `{python} rate(susp["cpi"])` [@ssuba2021]. April `{python} first["year"]`'s rise was set by that year's up-rating order [@uprating2011].

Centre: the rise, coloured by the figure that set it. Right: the level under the triple lock against earnings alone, CPI alone and the floor alone."
```{python}
F.history();
```

### If the plan had started earlier

The same comparison can be run backwards. Had the Burnham plan started in `{python} first_group["label"]`, the full new State Pension in `{python} fy(last_hist)` would be `{python} gbp(52 * past_weekly)` a year instead of the `{python} gbp(52 * actual_weekly)` paid, `{python} pct(100 * (1 - past_weekly / actual_weekly), 1)` lower (@fig-past). Most of the difference follows April `{python} spike["year"]`, when September CPI of `{python} rate(spike["cpi"])` set a rise far above earnings growth of `{python} rate(spike["earnings"])`. Started in `{python} listing([g["label"] for g in unchanged], "or")`, the plan would have paid the same as the triple lock every year. In full model runs, State Pension spending in `{python} fy(last_hist)` would have been `{python} bn(past_saving["gross"])` lower, and the government `{python} bn(past_saving["net"])` better off once tax and benefits respond.

```{python}
F.past_years();
```

## What the plan would save {#sec-budget}

```{python}
_law, _pub = D.EV["backtest"]["summary"]["suspended"], D.EV["backtest"]["summary"]["published"]
```

### The expected saving

@fig-fan shows the saving each year across the model's paths, and @tbl-expected the average with its Monte Carlo standard error. In `{python} fy(FINAL)` the expected saving is `{python} pm(g_final, 1)` in State Pension spending and `{python} pm(n_final, 1)` once income tax and benefits respond. Of the gross saving, extra Pension Credit takes back `{python} bn(comp["pension_credit"]["mean"])`, lower income tax `{python} bn(-comp["income_tax"]["mean"])` and extra Housing Benefit `{python} bn(comp["housing_benefit"]["mean"])`. In `{python} fy(MID)` the expected saving is `{python} bn(g_mid["mean"], 1)` gross and `{python} bn(n_mid["mean"], 1)` net.

The paths spread widely. In `{python} fy(FINAL)` the middle 80% of them save between `{python} bn(spread80[0], 1)` and `{python} bn(spread80[1], 1)` gross, and between `{python} bn(spread80n[0], 1)` and `{python} bn(spread80n[1], 1)` net. That spread lies within one model of prices and earnings: it describes the model's paths, not the odds of an outcome. The standard error is much smaller, because it measures only how precisely the full runs pin down the average. By `{python} fy(FINAL)` the full new State Pension is `{python} gbp(52 * gap["mean_gap_gbp_week"])` a year lower under the plan on average, and between `{python} gbp(52 * gap["gap_gbp_week"]["p10"])` and `{python} gbp(52 * gap["gap_gbp_week"]["p90"])` on the middle 80% of paths.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-expected

body = []
for y in [y for y in D.YEARS if y >= SWITCH]:
    g, n, l = D.est("gross", y), D.est("net", y), D.est("households_losing_pct", y)
    body.append([fy(y), num(g["mean"], 2), num(g["se"], 2), num(n["mean"], 2), num(n["se"], 2), pct(l["mean"]),
                 num(D.row(central, y)["gross"], 2)])
display(Markdown(md_table(["Year", "Gross", "SE", "Net", "SE", "Households with less income", "OBR central, gross"],
                          body)))
```

### Why the OBR's central forecast saves little

The OBR's central forecast is one smooth path. On it earnings beat CPI and the floor in almost every year after the switch, so the two rules give nearly the same rise and the plan saves `{python} bn(c_final["gross"], 1)` in `{python} fy(FINAL)` (`{python} bn(c_final["net"], 1)` net). Real years are bumpier. Whenever inflation spikes or earnings growth dips, the triple lock carries the higher rise forward and the plan does not, and since the saving can never be negative, every such year adds to it. That is why the average over many paths is far above the saving on the average path, and why we cost the plan over a distribution of paths (@sec-paths).

### Single scenarios

@fig-scenarios and @tbl-scenarios show four scenarios, each run in full under both rules. Two are single runs with no Monte Carlo error: the OBR central forecast, and the OBR's long-term path, on which the triple lock rises `{python} obr_premium` points a year faster than earnings. The other two take the simulated paths behind the expected saving and move calendar-year earnings growth `{python} V2["mean_path_pp"]` points a year lower or higher from 2031. Against the same paths without the shift, lower earnings growth changes the `{python} fy(FINAL)` saving by `{python} bn(sc_diff["minus"]["mean"], 1)` and higher by `{python} bn(sc_diff["plus"]["mean"], 1)``{python} ", which is within its Monte Carlo error" if sc_within["plus"] else ""`. The scenarios are named cases, not a range for the saving.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-scenarios

def _cell(v, se):
    return num(v, 1) if se is None else f"{num(v, 1)} ± {num(1.96 * se, 1)}"
body = []
for sc in D.scenarios([MID, FINAL]):
    vals = sc["values"]
    body.append([sc["name"], sc["kind"]] + [_cell(vals[y][k], vals[y][k + 2]) for y in (MID, FINAL) for k in (0, 1)])
```

### Weighting the paths to past volatility

The paths match the OBR's average forecast but keep the model's own year-to-year variation. They could instead be reweighted so that the variation of the gap between earnings and CPI, and how often the lead changes, match a past period [@robertson2005]. Reweighting the same full runs in this way gives an expected gross saving in `{python} fy(FINAL)` of `{python} bn(min(sens_g), 1)` to `{python} bn(max(sens_g), 1)` (@tbl-sensitivities in the appendix), against `{python} bn(g_final["mean"], 1)` for the paths as they are. We keep these as sensitivities: on past OBR forecasts the reweighted paths were further from what happened (@sec-test).

### Other costings {#sec-dwp}

```{python}
cov = D.R["coverage"]
cov_rows = {r["key"]: r for r in cov["rows"]}
sp_ratio = cov_rows["state_pension_bn"]["primary_gb_over_dwp"]
bmk = {b["id"]: b for b in D.R["benchmarks"]}
rf = bmk["rf_ratchet_2026_cumulative"]
rf_nums = re.findall(r"£(\d+(?:\.\d+)?)(?:bn| billion)", rf["figure_text"])
frs25 = re.search(r"£[\d.]+ billion", bmk["obr_frs_2025"]["figure_text"]).group(0)
```

DWP costs the plan at £`{python} dwp_nominal`bn in `{python} fy(FINAL)` in cash terms (£`{python} dwp_real`bn in 2025-26 prices) [@dwp_uprating2026], against our `{python} bn(g_final["mean"], 1)`. The figures differ for four reasons. DWP applies one uprating path, which it does not state; ours is an average over paths, and our high-saving path saves `{python} bn(D.row(p90, FINAL)["gross"], 1)`. DWP's model projects the population and each person's contribution record; we reweight today's survey (@sec-population). The survey's State Pension spending is `{python} pct(100 * (1 - sp_ratio), 0)` below DWP's matched figure (@tbl-coverage), and the gross saving scales with it. And DWP's figure is direct spending for Great Britain, which compares with our gross figure for Great Britain.

On our paths the triple lock rises `{python} points(prem["triple_lock"])` points a year faster than May–July earnings over the April rises of `{python} MID` to `{python} FINAL`, close to the OBR's assumption of `{python} obr_premium` points over its own earnings measure [@obr_lted2026]. Other published figures compare the triple lock with earnings uprating rather than with this plan, so they are context, not checks (@tbl-benchmarks). The OBR estimated that the triple lock would cost `{python} frs25` a year by 2029-30 against earnings uprating since 2012 [@obr_frs2025], and it projects State Pension spending to rise as a share of GDP over the long term, partly because of the triple lock [@obr_frs2026]. The Resolution Foundation puts the net saving from earnings uprating at about £`{python} rf_nums[1]`bn this year [@rf_ratchet2026]. The Institute for Fiscal Studies simulated the triple lock's cost from past inflation and earnings [@cribb2023], the closest precedent for our approach.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-benchmarks
#| tbl-cap: "Other published figures beside our closest figure. 'Like for like' says whether the two measure the same thing."
LIKE = {"yes": "Yes", "partial": "Partly", "no": "No"}
SHORT = {
    "dwp_uprating_2026": lambda b: f"£{dwp_nominal}bn saving in {fy(FINAL)}; Burnham plan vs triple lock, Great Britain, one path",
    "obr_lted_triple_lock_premium": lambda b: f"Triple lock rises {obr_premium} points a year faster than earnings (long-term assumption)",
    "obr_frs_2025": lambda b: f"Triple lock vs earnings uprating since 2012: {frs25} a year by 2029-30",
    "rf_ratchet_2026_cumulative": lambda b: f"Earnings-linked uprating since 2012: £{rf_nums[0]}bn gross, about £{rf_nums[1]}bn net, this year",
    "obr_frs_2026": lambda b: "Triple lock vs earnings uprating over a 50-year projection, % of GDP",
}
def ours(b):
    v = b["our_value"]
    return f"{points(v)} points a year" if "rate_minus_earnings" in b["our_metric"] else bn(v, 1)
body = [[f'{b["publisher"]} ({b["date"][:4]})', SHORT.get(b["id"], lambda b: b["figure_text"])(b), ours(b),
         LIKE[b["like_for_like"]]] for b in D.R["benchmarks"]]
display(Markdown(md_table(["Source", "Their figure", "Our closest figure", "Like for like"], body, "lllr")))
```

## One path in detail {#sec-paths}

```{python}
cp = D.CENTRAL["path"]
crows = D.path_rows(central)
a27 = cp["april_2027_inputs"]
floor_years = [r["year"] for r in crows if r["tl_source"] == "floor"]
after = [r for r in crows if r["year"] >= SWITCH]
first_earn = next(r for r in after if r["tl_source"] == "earnings")
differ = [r for r in crows if D.differs(r)]
cal_src = cp["calendar_source"]
efo_years = [int(y) for y, s in cal_src.items() if s == "efo_calendar"]
lted_years = [int(y) for y, s in cal_src.items() if s == "lted_converted"]
def gap_of(p):
    r = D.row(p, FINAL)
    return r["tl_weekly"] - r["bp_weekly"]
p50 = TYP
```

### The OBR central forecast

The central path uses the OBR's March 2026 Economic and fiscal outlook for calendar-year CPI and earnings growth in `{python} efo_years[0]`–`{python} efo_years[-1]` [@obr_efo2026] and its long-term economic determinants after that [@obr_lted2026], which the OBR describes as a projection, not a forecast. April 2027's rise uses the published May–July 2026 earnings growth, `{python} rate(a27["earnings"])`, and August 2026 CPI, `{python} rate(a27["cpi"])`, in place of September's, which ONS publishes on 21 October 2026.

Earnings grow by less than `{python} FLOOR` for several years, so the floor sets the triple lock in April `{python} listing(floor_years)`; from April `{python} first_earn["year"]` earnings lead every year (@fig-central). The two rules differ in `{python} words(len(differ))` years, April `{python} listing([r["year"] for r in differ])`: after the floor years the plan rises only by the floor, or by what brings it back to its earnings path, while the triple lock rises with earnings from the higher level. By `{python} fy(FINAL)` the full new State Pension is `{python} gbp(52 * c_final["tl_weekly"])` a year under the triple lock and `{python} gbp(52 * c_final["bp_weekly"])` under the plan, and the plan saves `{python} bn(c_final["gross"], 1)` (`{python} bn(c_final["net"], 1)` net).

```{python}
#| label: fig-central
#| fig-cap: "The two rules on the OBR central forecast. Left: the inputs behind each April's rise. Centre: the April rise under each rule; the dotted line marks the switch. Right: the level of the full new State Pension under each rule, and under earnings alone, CPI alone or the floor alone."
F.path_view("central");
```

### Simulated paths

The simulated paths come from a monthly model of prices and earnings, shifted so that their average matches the OBR's forecast (@sec-method). @fig-gaps shows how far apart the two rules end on four paths, and @tbl-paths what each saves. The typical path, nearest the middle of the distribution, saves `{python} bn(D.row(p50, FINAL)["gross"], 1)` in `{python} fy(FINAL)` (`{python} bn(D.row(p50, FINAL)["net"], 1)` net), close to the average; the high-saving path, at the 90th percentile, saves `{python} bn(D.row(p90, FINAL)["gross"], 1)`. Each is one path the model makes, not a forecast.

```{python}
#| label: fig-gaps
#| fig-cap: "How far the Burnham plan's full new State Pension ends below the triple lock's on each path shown, £ a year. The OBR central forecast and the example path lie close together near zero."
F.gaps();
```

```{python}
rows = []
for pid in D.PATH_IDS:
    p = D.path(pid)
    r = D.row(p, FINAL)
    rows.append([PATH_NAMES[pid][0].upper() + PATH_NAMES[pid][1:], gbp(52 * r["tl_weekly"]), gbp(52 * r["bp_weekly"]),
                 num(r["gross"], 2), num(r["net"], 2), pct(r["losing_pct"])])
display(Markdown(md_table(["Path", "Triple lock, £ a year", "Burnham plan, £ a year", "Gross", "Net",
                           "Households with less income"], rows, "lrrrrr")))
```

The household results run the typical path through PolicyEngine UK for the whole survey population, once under each rule. Every pensioner's State Pension is recalculated, and with it their income tax, Pension Credit, Housing Benefit, council tax reduction and Winter Fuel Payment.

### From gross to net

@tbl-account follows the gross saving on the typical path to the net saving. In `{python} fy(FINAL)` extra Pension Credit takes back `{python} bn(-acc["rows"][0][1])` of the `{python} bn(acc["gross"])` gross saving and lower income tax `{python} bn(-acc["rows"][5][1])`, leaving `{python} bn(acc["net"])` net, `{python} pct(100 * acc["net"] / acc["gross"], 0)` of the gross.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-account
#| tbl-cap: "From gross to net on the typical path in the final year, £ billion. Each offset is signed so the column adds up to the net saving."
body = [["Saving on the basic and new State Pension (gross)", num(acc["gross"], 2)]]
body += [[label, num(v, 2)] for label, v in acc["rows"]]
body.append(["Everything else (other taxes and benefits)", num(acc["other"], 2)])
body.append(["**Saving to the government (net)**", f'**{num(acc["net"], 2)}**'])
display(Markdown(md_table(["", fy(FINAL)], body)))
```

### Who has less income

Averaged over all paths, `{python} pct(lose_final["mean"], 0)` of UK households have less income than under the triple lock in `{python} fy(FINAL)`, and the share is about the same on every path: it is set by who receives a State Pension, not by the size of the gap. On the typical path those households have `{python} gbp(aff["mean_loss_gbp"])` a year less on average. Relative to income, the change is largest in the `{python} ordinal(low_dec["decile"])` income decile, at `{python} pct(abs(low_dec["pct_income_change"]), 2)` of income (@fig-deciles).

On the OBR central forecast, where the pension gap is small, no poverty measure changes by more than `{python} num(pov_c_max, 2)` percentage points. On the typical path pensioner poverty after housing costs is `{python} num(pov_typ_abs, 1)` points higher on the absolute measure and `{python} num(pov_typ_rel, 1)` points higher on the relative one, while poverty among everyone changes by `{python} num(max(abs(pov_change(TYP, k)) for k in ("everyone_absolute_ahc", "everyone_relative_ahc")), 1)` points or less (@tbl-poverty). Pension Credit makes up much of a lower pension for pensioners on the guarantee, but not for those just above it.

```{python}

#| fig-cap: "The change in household income under the Burnham plan against the triple lock, by income decile, on the typical path in the final year, % of income."
F.deciles("monthly_p50");
```

Four example pensioners, run as households under each rule on the typical path, show how tax and benefits pass on a lower State Pension (@tbl-pensioners, @fig-pensioners). Each receives the full flat-rate State Pension and claims everything it is entitled to. They are hypothetical households, not survey records. A lower State Pension means less income tax for a pensioner above the personal allowance and more Pension Credit for one entitled to it; Pension Credit counts income after tax [@spc2002], and council tax reduction disregards the income of a pensioner receiving the guarantee credit [@si2012_2885]. In `{python} fy(FINAL)` the share of the lower pension felt as lower income is `{python} listing([f"{share_words(s)} for ({letter[k]})" for k, _, s in ex_rows])`.

## Method {#sec-method}

### Model and data

Every fiscal and household figure is a full run of PolicyEngine UK [@policyengine_py; @policyengine_uk] on the whole survey population, once under each rule; nothing is scaled from another run. All runs use one release: policyengine `{python} V2["policyengine"]`, which pins policyengine-uk `{python} V2["policyengine_uk"]` and policyengine-core `{python} V2["policyengine_core"]` and is published with the Enhanced Family Resources Survey for `{python} fy(2024)`, release `{python} V2["data"]` (`{python} count(D.R["coverage"]["datasets"]["primary"]["records"]["households"])` households). A path's CPI and earnings growth replace the model's economic assumptions before the data load, so benefit rates, tax thresholds and earnings follow it, and every run checks that they do. Only the basic and new State Pension differ between the two runs of a path. Under both rules the additional State Pension rises with September CPI, the Pension Credit guarantee with May–July earnings, and State Pension age follows the law's timetable. Money is in cash terms, for the UK. The results were built at revision `{python} D.PROV["git_revision"][:7]` of PolicyEngine/uk-triple-lock and read from its `data/results.json`; the file holds no survey record's identifier, weight or amount.

### Paths of prices and earnings

```{python}
m = D.EV["draws"]["model"]
```

The paths come from a model of monthly changes in the CPI index [@ons_d7bt] and in average weekly earnings [@ons_kab9], fitted to data from 2000 to the latest published month, with the furlough months of 2020–21 left out. Each simulated month draws a pair of past shocks together, so prices and earnings keep their joint variation. From the simulated months come both the statutory inputs (September CPI, May–July earnings growth) and the calendar-year growth the rest of the model uses. Every path is then shifted by the same smooth drift so that the average matches the OBR's forecast in every year, while each path keeps its own ups and downs.

### Averaging over the paths

The model makes `{python} N_PATHS` paths, and the rules give each path's gap in the full new State Pension before any model run. Paths on which the two rules pay the same every year save nothing. The rest are split into `{python} words(len(D.EV["strata"]))` equal groups by that gap, and `{python} N_RUNS` paths drawn across the groups, more where the gap varies most [@neyman1934], are run in full. The expected saving weights each group's average by its share of the paths, and its standard error comes from the spread within groups.

### The population in each year {#sec-population}

The survey is a sample of households in `{python} fy(2024)`. Each record stands for a person of its age in every year. After `{python} V2["anchor_year"]`, the year the data release calibrates to, household weights are reweighted so that each age and sex group grows as in the ONS's 2024-based population projection [@ons_npp2024]. Survey ages are top-coded at `{python} V2["top_code"]`; records at the top code are spread across ages up to `{python} V2["age_cap"]` in line with ONS single-year shares. Each person's State Pension type follows from their date of birth: those who reached State Pension age before 6 April 2016 are on the basic State Pension, later cohorts on the new one [@pa2014]. Deaths, migration and contribution histories are not simulated.

### Testing the model on past forecasts {#sec-test}

An expected saving needs a model whose paths behave like the real inputs. Before scoring any model we committed a test on past OBR forecasts [@obr_hofd2026]: fitted only on data available before each forecast, does the model's central 80% band contain what then happened, in the gap between earnings and CPI each year and in the gap the two rules open after four rises? April 2022 is scored as the law applied it, with the earnings leg suspended. A first version of the test, which scored April 2022 on the published earnings, failed every model because of the furlough effect on 2021 pay; we changed it after seeing those scores and report both. In a dry run on today's data the model passes: the outcome fell inside its range in `{python} words(dry["terminal_hits"])` of `{python} words(dry["terminal_origins"])` final years and `{python} pct(100 * dry["annual_coverage"], 0)` of annual checks (@tbl-screen in the appendix). The binding test runs on the inputs available after the 28 October 2026 Budget. If the model passes, the expected saving stands; if not, the update removes it and keeps the single scenarios.

## Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

The Burnham plan keeps the triple lock's protection against prices and its `{python} FLOOR` floor, but not its carry-forward of years in which prices or the floor beat earnings. Its saving therefore depends on how often the lead passes between prices and earnings, not only on their expected growth. On the OBR's smooth central forecast the plan saves `{python} bn(c_final["gross"], 1)` in `{python} fy(FINAL)`; averaged over the model's paths it saves `{python} bn(g_final["mean"], 1)` in State Pension spending and `{python} bn(n_final["mean"], 1)` after tax and benefits respond, with a wide spread between paths.

About `{python} pct(lose_final["mean"], 0)` of households, nearly all with a pensioner, have less income than under the triple lock, with Pension Credit and income tax making up part of the difference; on the typical path pensioner poverty after housing costs rises by `{python} num(max(pov_typ_abs, pov_typ_rel), 1)` percentage points or less. The wider lesson applies to any uprating rule that takes the highest of several indices: its cost depends on how the indices vary, and costing it on a single central path can understate it. These figures are provisional until the binding test on the 28 October 2026 Budget forecast.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-screen
#| tbl-cap: "The test on past forecasts, dry run on today's inputs: share of outcomes inside each model's central 80% band, by test and model, with April 2022 scored as in law (which decides the verdict) and as published (for reference)."
scr = D.R["uncertainty_screen"]

                         ("Pass" if verdict["passes"] else "Fail") if t == "suspended" else "Reference",
                         pct(100 * r["annual_gap_coverage"]["mean"], 0),
                         f'{r["terminal_coverage"]["hits"]} of {r["terminal_scored_origins"]}'])
```
